newsitem.title: FRANCE: French growth seen falling short of government hopes - poll.
newsitem.headline: French growth seen falling short of government hopes - poll.

text.p: French economic growth is seen falling short of the government's target this year and unemployment, already at record levels, could set new peaks in 1997, a Reuter poll of 25 economists published on Tuesday showed.

Yet more than half of those polled forecast a budget deficit at three percent of gross domestic product which economists said reflected the growing conviction that the government will do what it takes to hit the target to join European economic and monetary union.

France needs to cut its public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year from four percent in 1996 in order to meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria to join a single European currency in 1999.

In a previous Reuter poll conducted in October less than a third expected the deficit to be at three percent and only two out of 13 economists predicted France would meet the target in the poll last January.

The median forecast, the midpoint of the range, for GDP in 1997 was 2.1, unchanged from the October survey and the median forecast for the unemployment rate was 12.8 percent, up from 12.5 percent in October and 11.4 percent a year ago.
Unemployment reached a record 12.7 percent in December, the latest month for which figures are available.

David Naude, economist at JP Morgan in Paris, forecast growth of 1.8 percent, well below the government's 2.3 percent target, and an unemployment rate of 12.9 percent but said he had no doubt the deficit target would be met.

"I'm just being consistent with what we've seen from the government. The deficit outcome has had little to do with growth," Naude said. "They've shown they have enough resources to get the deficit to three percent."
France this year will use 37 billion francs ($6.7 billion) in pension fund money being transferred from state-owned France Telecom ahead of partial privatisation to reach its three percent target.
Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris, said his forecast of 3.1 percent was above three percent to take account of a risk welfare spending would be higher than expected.
"But 3.1 would be enough for France to participate in the first wave of monetary union," he said.

The most pessimistic forecast was from the COE economic forecasting unit of the Paris Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The private body said it saw the public deficit at 3.5 percent but said France would still be allowed to join monetary union.

The poll showed the key intervention rate, which sets the floor for French money market rates, will be trimmed further, but not by much. The median forecast for the next four quarters was three percent compared with 3.15 percent currently.

Economists said one of the main surprises of 1996 had been the surge in the size of the labour force and even if growth were to create jobs in 1997 the unemployment rate would probably still climb in 1997.
"A rise of 80,000 jobs won't be enough to cut the rate," said Mange. "Last year was special...but we still need more than 160,000 jobs to be created to stop the rise in unemployment."
"The labour force is growing quite rapidly in France due to demographics and it will continue to push the unemployment rate higher," Naude said.
Trade will continue to help the French economy during the next two years. The median forecast for the current account surplus was 94 billion francs in 1997 and 90 billion in 1998.

As in previous surveys HSBC James Capel stood out from the crowd. Their prediction that monetary union will be delayed or abandoned led to diverging forecasts for three month rates and the spread between French and German bond yields.

The median forecast for the spread between 10-year yields was zero from October 1997 right through to 1999 but HSBC predicted French yields would be 0.70 percentage point higher than German yields by the first quarter of 1998.
HSBC also forecast the gap between the French intervention rate and three-month money would open out to 1.85 percentage points by the end of the year from 0.25 now.

"It's reflecting the fact in our central European forecast EMU won't go ahead, which explains why three month money is being driven up," HSBC James Capel economist Gwyn Hacche said. "The authorities will leave the floor where it is and only act on the rate ceiling."

Their assumption is that the Bank of France would be forced to raise rates in the event of a failure of monetary union, to protect the franc, which they see as falling to 3.70 per mark at the end of 1997 from around 3.37 per mark now. ($1=5.523 French Franc)
